source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19(3):265-288
finding: Takes the cockpit, not the pilot, as the unit of analysis. The cockpit system 'remembers' landing speeds by building and saving representational states across media (speed card, voice, speed bugs, pilot heads).
numbers: Based on more than 100 observed flights as an observer member of crews, plus training in 747-400, MD-80 and A320 ground schools. Account is 'stylized', with no extended transcripts and no statistics.
limits: Ethnographic and stylized, not an experiment. No measured error rates. Generalisation rests on the author's judgement.
agent_relevance: Memory for a plan can live in the artefacts and the procedure, not in the agent. For our agent: state written to a durable, checkable store beats state held only in the context.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19(3):265-288
finding: Three descriptions of one activity: procedural (what a pilot would say), external representations and processes (observable), and internal representations (inferred). The external description constrains the internal one.
numbers: Observable media listed: gross weight display, speed card booklet, two airspeed indicators with bugs, flight guidance speed window, spoken exchanges. Pilot memories are 'additional media'.
limits: Internal description is inferred; Hutchins admits 'lacking additional evidence, we cannot know the duration or quality of these memories'.
agent_relevance: Method to copy: describe the agent's run first as external artefacts and transitions, then ask what the model must hold internally. The schema states are the external description.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19(3):265-288
finding: Speed bugs do not help pilots remember. They reorganise the task: scale reading plus remembered numbers becomes a judgment of spatial proximity between needle and bug.
numbers: Salmon-bug base is about 10 knots wide, so 'needle on the bug body' means within 5 knots of Vref. Call-out rule: deviation of more than plus or minus 5 knots. 500 ft call example: 'Five hundred feet, plus four, seven down'.
quote: Speed bugs do not help pilots remember speeds; rather, they are part of the process by which the cockpit system remembers speeds.
limits: Interpretation by the author. No comparison against a no-bug crew is reported.
agent_relevance: A good check turns a hard cognitive step (mental arithmetic, recall) into an easy perceptual or code-checked one. Prefer checks the program evaluates over checks the model must reason out.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19(3):265-288
finding: Cognitive work is moved across time, social space and modality. Speeds are computed in a low workload phase (descent, before 18,000 ft), saved on the bugs, used 10 to 15 minutes later. The pilot not flying turns a visual deviation into a spoken one so the pilot flying keeps eyes outside.
numbers: Weights come in about 2,000 lb card increments. A set bug is 'much less likely than a pilot's memory to forget its value'. Final approach: call-outs at 500 ft and whenever speed deviates more than 5 knots.
limits: Claim about robustness to interruption is argued, not measured here.
agent_relevance: Do planning and computation in a quiet early state and store the result; later states read it, not recompute it. Matches state-bound operators with saved outputs.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19(3):265-288
finding: The system is deliberately redundant: redundant representation, redundant processing and redundant checking. Mandatory callouts and cross-checks ('Set on the left and cross-checked') let one pilot catch the other's wrong bug or wrong weight card.
numbers: Challenge-response item: 'Flight instruments and bugs / Set and cross-checked'. Two airspeed indicators; speed card posted a few inches from the gross-weight display so a wrong-weight pick is visible. Author never saw a crew fail to set approach speeds in all observations; it is a 'killer' item.
limits: Redundancy is partly a by-product: the flap call by PF and handle move by PNF was introduced to free the pilot's hands, and cross-checking came as a side effect.
agent_relevance: Cross-checks work because the two checkers hold different views of the same fact. Two samples from one model are not that (see G4). Use different channels: code, a held-out test, a second representation.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19(3):265-288
finding: Structure in the environment gives more than extra memory. Experts use affordances the designers never planned, such as the width of the salmon bug as a yardstick.
numbers: Engineer for the Boeing 757/767 airspeed indicator confirmed the base width is not in the specification; it fits between the large ticks at 10-knot intervals.
limits: One anecdote, but it is the central evidence for opportunistic use of structure.
agent_relevance: Leave room for the agent to use artefact structure it was not told about, such as file layout, test output format, checklist order.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19(3):265-288 (discussion)
finding: Individual-memory theory is not enough: it explains why the system needs so many components outside the pilots, not how the system works.
numbers: Cockpit memory is 'not made primarily of pilot memory'. It is a mix of recognition, recall, pattern matching, cross-modality checking, construction and reconstruction.
limits: A strong claim; critics dispute whether this is 'cognition' or only tool use (see other angles).
agent_relevance: Do not judge the agent only by what the model 'knows'; judge the model plus its scaffold as one system.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks. Cognitive Science 18(1):87-122
finding: Framework of distributed representations: a task's representational system is a set of internal and external representations that together carry the abstract task structure. Method: decompose a hierarchical task into levels and test each level.
numbers: Four experiments on Tower of Hanoi isomorphs (cups/coffee and objects). Exp 1A: 24 undergraduates, all rules internal, conditions with 1 to 4 rules. Exp 1B: 24, all but one rule external. Exp 2: 18. Exp 3: 36.
limits: Student samples; small N per condition; time, steps and errors normalised by minimum steps. Exact means are shown only in figures.
agent_relevance: Where a rule lives (memory vs the physical object) changes difficulty. For the agent, rules the code enforces cost no working memory; rules written in the prompt do.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks (Exp 1A and 1B)
finding: With all rules internal, the middle problem (II23, three rules) was hardest; with all but one rule external, difficulty rose steadily with the number of rules. Same abstract problem, different order of difficulty.
numbers: Minimum steps 2, 4, 7, 8 for the 4 conditions. Exp 1A order easiest to hardest by time and errors: II < II3 < II234 and II23 (II234 vs II23 not significant). Exp 1B: II < II-E3 <= II-E23 <= II-E234. Hardest vs easiest solution time ratio up to one to ten. Exp 1B had no errors at all.
limits: Order of difficulty differed by measure (time, steps, errors); several pairs not significant (p > .3).
agent_relevance: Difficulty is not a property of the abstract task. The same logic can be hard or easy by representation, so changing the format of a prompt can change success without changing the problem.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks (Exp 2)
finding: The more rules were externalised, the easier the problem. External rules were error-proof; every error was on an internal rule.
numbers: 18 undergraduates, 54 games. Hardest to easiest: II23 > II2-E3, about equal to II-E23. Main effects p < .05 (time, steps), p < .005 (errors). Errors on external rules: zero. In 52 of 54 games the last three steps took 3 steps.
quote: external rules seem to be error proof: subjects did not make any errors for external rules
limits: Small N. II2-E3 vs II-E23 not significant. Direction agrees with Kotovsky, Hayes and Simon (1985), who only reported solution times.
agent_relevance: Rules put in physical or code constraints cannot be broken; rules put in text can. Supports guardrails as code, not as advice.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks (Exp 3)
finding: Dimensional representation matters: the same ordinal or nominal dimension is easier when carried by location than by size or colour.
numbers: 36 undergraduates. Ordinal dimension: location better than size and color on time and errors (p < .01 time for size vs location; p < .03 errors). Nominal dimension: location better than size and color on time and errors; size vs color not different.
limits: Differences in solution steps mostly not significant. Some statistics were garbled in the text copy I used.
agent_relevance: The carrier (position vs label) is itself a design variable; try a spatial or tabular form of state when a label form fails.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research. ACM TOCHI 7(2):174-196
finding: Two principles define the approach: (1) the unit of analysis is set by functional relations among elements, not skin and skull; (2) the mechanisms include external, material and social ones. Three kinds of distribution: across people, between internal and external structure, and through time (products of earlier events change later events).
numbers: Pre-publication revision dated 23 April 2000. Method loop: cognitive ethnography, theory, experiment, design, new ethnography.
quote: A cognitive process is delimited by the functional relationships among the elements that participate in it
limits: Review and position paper, not new data. Authors admit cognitive ethnography leaves inferences 'under-constrained by the available data'.
agent_relevance: The third kind (through time) is our scaffold: earlier states leave artefacts that shape later states.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research (opportunistic structure)
finding: Experts use environmental structure in ways designers did not foresee, found only by observation. Example: pilots display the weather radar test pattern as a reminder that a final fuel transfer is in progress. In lab work on Tetris, players use actions that change the world to ease thinking.
numbers: Cites Kirsh & Maglio on epistemic vs pragmatic action. Children building models from small parts modularise in ways that help then and are dismantled later.
limits: Anecdotal example, no frequency given.
agent_relevance: Allow the agent explicit epistemic actions (probe, print, test a guess) as normal moves, not as wasted steps.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action. Cognitive Science 18(4):513-549
finding: In Tetris, some rotations and translations are best explained as actions that change the world to make the problem easier (epistemic), not to carry out a plan (pragmatic). A standard sequential information-processing model of Tetris cannot explain human performance data, even when sequential processing is relaxed.
numbers: Abstract only (via Crossref). No numbers in the abstract.
limits: I read the abstract only, not the full text. Exact timings not recorded; do not quote numbers from this entry.
agent_relevance: Actions that look wasteful (extra probe calls, scratch computation) can be the cheapest way to cut uncertainty. Budget rules should not ban them.

source: Norman (1991) Cognitive artifacts. In Carroll (ed) Designing interaction, pp. 17-38; Norman (1993) Things that make us smart
finding: Defines cognitive artefacts as artificial devices designed to maintain, display or operate upon information to serve a representational function. Artefacts change the task rather than only amplify the person.
numbers: Seen only as a bibliographic record and a quoted definition in a search summary. Full text not found open.
quote: designed to maintain, display, or operate upon information in order to serve a representational function
limits: Not opened. The personal-view vs system-view claim is not verified in this session.
agent_relevance: Our checklist and state machine are cognitive artefacts in this sense: they change the task the model faces.

source: Degani & Wiener (1990) Human factors of flight-deck checklists: the normal checklist. NASA CR-177549
finding: Field study of airline checklists using NTSB (1983-1988 accidents, 1969-1988 recommendations) and ASRS (1981-1989) data plus interviews. A checklist is a memory guide and a coordinator of tasks; it is vulnerable and was long neglected.
numbers: Three accidents in 15 months had checklist misuse as a probable cause: Air New Orleans BAe J-31, Northwest 255 (MD-80, Detroit, no-flap/no-slat takeoff) and Delta 1141 (B-727, Dallas-Fort Worth, same). 71-page report.
limits: Case and report based; no controlled trial of checklist designs. ASRS reports are voluntary and self-selected.
agent_relevance: Our checks fail the same way: they get skipped under interruption, not because the rule is unknown.

source: Degani & Wiener (1990) Human factors of flight-deck checklists: the normal checklist (methods)
finding: Two main methods of running a checklist: challenge-response (read item, other checks and answers) and do-list (call-do-response). Challenge-response gives mutual redundancy and is dominant, but in two-pilot cockpits some airlines let one pilot challenge and answer himself, removing the redundancy.
numbers: Several flight management officials interviewed said the quality of the procedure in the two-pilot cockpit is 'below expected standards'. Do-lists are detailed and time consuming.
limits: Opinion of interviewees; no error rates by method in the report.
agent_relevance: A self-checking model (same author as checker) is the single-pilot checklist: weaker than an independent checker. Supports code-run checks over model self-check.

source: Degani & Wiener (1990) Human factors of flight-deck checklists: the normal checklist (Northwest 255, distractions)
finding: Interruption broke the checklist. The TAXI checklist at Detroit was usually done 1 to 2 minutes after the plane moved; on flight 255 several interruptions (new weather, runway data) meant it was not done in that window, and the external cues that start it were gone.
numbers: Monan (1979) ASRS study of distraction: 169 air carrier distraction reports, 22 labelled as distractions caused by checklist procedures. NTSB 1988a quoted on missing external cues.
limits: Single accident narrative plus a small report count.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on the model to remember to run a check; trigger it from state (code), because a check that depends on a cue in the middle of other work gets lost.

source: Pronovost et al. (2006) An intervention to decrease catheter-related bloodstream infections in the ICU. NEJM 355:2725-32
finding: A checklist-based evidence programme in Michigan ICUs cut catheter-related bloodstream infection sharply and the drop was sustained.
numbers: 108 ICUs agreed, 103 reported; 1,981 ICU-months, 375,757 catheter-days. Median rate 2.7 per 1,000 catheter-days at baseline to 0 at 3 months (P <= 0.002). Mean 7.7 to 1.4 at 16-18 months (P < 0.002). Incidence rate ratio 0.62 (0.47-0.81) at 0-3 months; 0.34 (0.23-0.50) at 16-18 months.
limits: Before-after cohort, no control group; secular trends possible. The abstract page I read does not list the checklist items; the programme included more than a checklist (culture, feedback).
agent_relevance: Strong case for checklists, but the effect comes with a package. A check alone is not the whole system.

source: Haynes et al. (2009) A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population. NEJM 360:491-9
finding: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist introduced at 8 hospitals in 8 cities was followed by lower death and complication rates.
numbers: Before: 3,733 patients; after: 3,955 patients (noncardiac surgery, age 16 or older). Death 1.5% to 0.8% (P=0.003). Inpatient complications 11.0% to 7.0% (P<0.001). Oct 2007 to Sept 2008.
limits: Before-after design, no concurrent control; sites self-selected; the later Ontario natural experiment did not reproduce the effect.
agent_relevance: The headline result for 'checklists work' in practice. Treat as an upper bound.

source: Urbach et al. (2014) Introduction of surgical safety checklists in Ontario, Canada. NEJM 370:1029-38
finding: Failed replication at scale: after mandated adoption in Ontario hospitals there was no significant fall in operative death or complications.
limits: Observational before/after in 3-month windows; checklist use was encouraged by policy and compliance and quality were not observed. Others criticised the methods (second-hand). Uptake and fidelity are likely causes.
agent_relevance: A checklist that is not truly used, or is a box-ticking ritual, gives nothing. Our checks must run on real output and bind the next transition, not be advisory.

source: Systematic review 2024: The role of WHO surgical checklists in reducing postoperative adverse outcomes (via Europe PMC)
finding: Systematic review of WHO checklist studies: of 93 studies reaching full assessment, 13 were of enough quality; 10 reported complications and 9 of those found a drop after adoption.
numbers: 17,821 titles screened, 93 retrieved, 13 included.
limits: I read a truncated abstract from the Europe PMC API; the mortality count was cut off. Studies are mostly before-after.
agent_relevance: Evidence for checklists is positive but mostly weak in design, and mixed in large natural experiments.

source: Cook, Rocktaeschel, Foerster, Aumiller, Wang (2024) TICKing all the boxes: generated checklists improve LLM evaluation and generation. arXiv 2410.03608
finding: LLM-generated YES/NO checklists, one requirement each, improve judging and generation without training.
numbers: Exact agreement of LLM judgments with human preference rose from 46.4% to 52.2% (checklist vs direct score). Self-refinement with the same checklist: +7.8 points on LiveBench reasoning. Best-of-N by checklist: +6.3 points on WildBench. Human annotator agreement rose from 0.194 to 0.256 with checklists shown.
limits: Abstract page read, not the full paper. Checklists and judging come from an LLM, so they inherit judge bias; gains are benchmark points, not safety outcomes.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of 'checklist as artefact' for LLMs. Atomic yes/no items beat holistic scoring; but items are written and judged by the model.

source: Viswanathan et al. (2025) Checklists are better than reward models for aligning language models (RLCF). arXiv 2507.18624, NeurIPS 2025
finding: Reinforcement learning from checklist feedback (instruction-specific checklists graded by a 72B judge plus verifier programs) improves a 7B model on every instruction-following benchmark tried, where other AI feedback was mixed.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: +5.4% relative on FollowBench hard satisfaction (4 points), +6.9% relative on InFoBench (6 points), +6.4% relative on Arena-Hard (3 points win rate). WildChecklists: 130,000 instructions. Candidate-based vs direct checklists (manual, 50 items): atomicity 90.0 vs 68.0, overall preferred 56.0 vs 38.0.
limits: Strong-to-weak: judge is Qwen2.5-72B. Scoring took about 4 days on eight H100 GPUs for 130k instructions (authors). Only preference-based RL tried. This is training, not an inference scaffold.
agent_relevance: Checklists work as a reward signal. The lesson for us is that item quality (objective, atomic) matters and that seeing candidate answers before writing the list improved it. Caution: such lists depend on model output, so they are not independent.

source: Ebouky, Bartezzaghi, Rigotti (2025) Eliciting reasoning in language models with cognitive tools. arXiv 2506.12115
finding: Four modular 'cognitive tools' (understand question, recall related, examine answer, backtracking), each run by the model as a tool call, raise maths accuracy without training. Close to Norman's idea that a tool restructures the task.
numbers: Smolbenchmark pass@1 averaged over 16 runs, baseline to best tool: Qwen2.5-7B 75.8 to 80.5; Qwen2.5-32B 79.6 to 84.2; Llama3.1-8B 48.7 to 59.4; Llama3.3-70B 52.8 to 79.5. AIME 2024: GPT-4.1 32.0 to 53.0 (cognitive prompting 42.0); o1-preview 44.6. Qwen2.5-32B AIME 17.2 to 32.1.
limits: Gains are uneven: Qwen2.5-7B AIME 12.5 to 14.6 (within noise); Llama3.1-8B MATH500 50.7 with tools vs 53.3 for plain CoT. Tools are run by the same model, so no independent check.
agent_relevance: Tool-per-operation design matches our O1-O8 operators. Gains are model and benchmark specific; test on our own tasks.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet. ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2310.01798)
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to review its answer does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels it looks large, which is why earlier reports overstated it.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic self-correction: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (3 calls) to 74.7 (5 calls); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3 (my reading of a garbled table).
limits: Table columns partly garbled by PDF extraction, so row labels of the oracle table are my reading. HotpotQA used 100 test examples. This is intrinsic self-review, not tool or code checks.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G2 and G5: a checklist the model ticks itself is the one-pilot cockpit. It needs an external signal.

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2023) Chain-of-Verification reduces hallucination in large language models. arXiv 2309.11495
finding: Draft, plan verification questions, answer them in a separate context, then revise. Verification that cannot see the first draft works best, because it avoids copying the draft's mistakes.
numbers: Llama 65B Wikidata list precision: few-shot 0.17, CoVe joint 0.29, two-step 0.36, factored 0.32. FACTSCORE long-form 60.8 (joint) to 63.7 (factored).
quote: verifying questions should not attend to the original baseline response as they may be prone to repeating it
limits: Hallucination of facts, not reasoning; the authors say CoT is less suited here. Llama 65B, 2023 models. Table text partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Fits 'two pilots with different views': the checker must not attend to the draft. Supports independent check contexts.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show your work: scratchpads for intermediate computation with language models. arXiv 2112.00114
finding: A written scratchpad, an external trace the model can read back, lets transformers do multi-step computation they fail at in one pass. The scratchpad is the model's own cognitive artefact.
numbers: Polynomial evaluation: few-shot direct 8.8% vs scratchpad 20.1%; fine-tuning direct 31.8% vs scratchpad 50.7%. Program execution: direct 11% / 20% vs scratchpad 26.5% / 41.5%. Out-of-distribution 9-10 digit addition: models without scratchpad fail completely.
limits: Small 2021 models; fine-tuned or few-shot; scratchpad format designed by hand. Absolute tracing accuracy still low.
agent_relevance: The simplest artefact result for LLMs: externalising intermediate state changes what the model can do, as speed bugs change what pilots must hold.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction. arXiv 2406.01297
finding: Survey: prior self-correction work often over-evaluates it with unfair setups; success needs reliable external feedback or fine-tuning, not prompted self-review alone.
numbers: No table figures extracted. It cites negative results from Huang et al. 2024, Tyen et al. 2024 and Hong et al. 2024 on self-detection of mistakes.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read.
agent_relevance: Backs the rule that revision is triggered by external output, which is the cockpit cross-check logic.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds. Cognitive Science 19(3):265-288 (design detail)
finding: The speed card booklet is a durable memory and gross weight acts as a filter on it. Weight and speeds are printed on the same card, so choosing the card by weight selects the speeds, and the computation is built into the object.
numbers: MD-80 cards in about 2,000 lb steps; example card for 122,000 lb lists maneuvering speeds (0/RET 227 down to 40 at 137) and Vref (28/EXT 132, 40/EXT 128). Frequent speeds in larger font; box around Vref.
limits: Design commentary; the transposition-error remark is attributed to Norman 1991 and Wickens & Flach 1988, not measured.
agent_relevance: Put the key and its answer in the same record. Example: store each check together with the output it checked.
